title: Encryption: Hashes, Keys, Signatures and TLS
sub: Break a classical cipher, use hashes, MACs, AES-GCM and signatures correctly, build your own certificate authority and read a TLS 1.3 handshake
goals: Tell encoding, hashing, MACs, encryption and signatures apart, and choose the right one for a job
Verify downloads with SHA-256 and store passwords with a salted, slow hash
Encrypt and decrypt with AES-GCM, and explain why a reused nonce is catastrophic
Explain key exchange and signatures, and sign and verify files with your SSH key
Build a private CA, serve HTTPS with it, and read every step of a TLS 1.3 handshake

blocks.text: Cryptography is what lets you type a password on café Wi-Fi, download software you can trust, push code with a key instead of a     password, and call an API that nobody can tamper with in transit. You do not need the mathematics to use it well, but you do need the     vocabulary, a feel for what each tool guarantees and, above all, the rules for not misusing it. In this chapter you will break a     classical cipher, watch hashes and authenticated encryption behave, agree on a secret in public, sign and verify files with your SSH     key, build your own certificate authority and serve HTTPS with it, and look inside a TLS 1.3 handshake message by message.

blocks.title: The first rule: do not invent your own

blocks.text: Every primitive in this chapter is easy to call and easy to misuse: a reused nonce, a missing authentication tag, a     password stored with a fast hash. Use high-level, maintained tools and libraries (TLS, SSH, age, libsodium, your platform's crypto API)     and treat home-made schemes as a learning exercise only, never as protection for anything real.
Four tools that are often confused

blocks.title: What each one is for

blocks.code:
import base64, hashlib

secret = "hunter2"
encoded = base64.b64encode(secret.encode()).decode()
print("base64:", encoded, "->", base64.b64decode(encoded).decode())   # anyone can reverse it
print("sha256:", hashlib.sha256(secret.encode()).hexdigest())
print("sha256 of a 1 MB file is still", len(hashlib.sha256(b"x" * 1_000_000).hexdigest()), "hex characters")
blocks.out:
base64: aHVudGVyMg== -> hunter2
sha256: f52fbd32b2b3b86ff88ef6c490628285f482af15ddcb29541f94bcf526a3f6c7
sha256 of a 1 MB file is still 64 hex characters

blocks.text: If a tutorial "encrypts" a password with base64, close the tab: base64 is a way of writing bytes as text and protects     nothing. Security goals are usually summarised as **CIA**: **c**onfidentiality (only the right people read it), **i**ntegrity (nobody     changed it unnoticed) and **a**uthenticity (it came from who it claims). Pick the tool by the goal.
Why classical ciphers fail

A Caesar cipher shifts every letter by a fixed amount. It has only 26 keys, and worse, it keeps the *pattern* of the language:     the most common ciphertext letter is almost certainly `e` shifted. Modern ciphers are designed so the output looks like random bytes     whatever the input, and the key space is so large that trying every key is impossible. Break the Caesar text in the lab below, then     switch tabs to see what modern tools do differently.

blocks.title: Crack a Caesar cipher automatically

task.text: Write `crack(ciphertext)` that returns `(shift, plaintext)` for the shift (0 to 25) whose decryption contains the most of the words        in `COMMON`. Keep letter case and leave non-letters alone. Then crack `MSG` and print the plaintext.

hints: Write `shift_text(text, k)` first and check that shifting by `k` then `-k` gives the original back.
Score each of the 26 candidates by counting words that are in `COMMON`, then take the `max`.

why.text: Twenty-six candidates and a crude English detector are enough. This is the core of all brute-force attacks: if a computer can        enumerate the keys and recognise success, the cipher is broken. Modern keys are 128 or 256 bits, so enumerating them is not a question        of faster computers but of more energy than the Sun will produce.

blocks.check:
k, p = crack(MSG)
assert k == 13, "The shift for MSG is 13 (ROT13). Got " + repr(k)
assert p == "Never send passwords in the clear. Use a password manager.", "Keep case and punctuation. Got: " + p
k2, p2 = crack("Wkh vhfuhw lv lq wkh qdph.")
assert (k2, p2) == (3, "The secret is in the name."), "crack() must work for any shift, not just 13"
assert "Never send passwords" in out, "Print the plaintext of MSG"

blocks.text: Hashes: fingerprints for data

A cryptographic **hash** turns any input into a fixed-size digest (32 bytes for SHA-256) so that you cannot run it backwards,     cannot find two inputs with the same digest, and any change to the input, even one bit, changes about half the output bits. That last     property is the **avalanche effect**, and it is what makes a hash a reliable fingerprint:

blocks.code:
import hashlib

def bits_differ(a: bytes, b: bytes) -> int:
    return sum(bin(x ^ y).count("1") for x, y in zip(a, b))

a, b = b"hello", b"hellO"             # 'o' (0x6f) and 'O' (0x4f) differ in one bit
ha, hb = hashlib.sha256(a).digest(), hashlib.sha256(b).digest()
print(ha.hex())
print(hb.hex())
print("input bits that differ: ", bits_differ(a, b))
print("output bits that differ:", bits_differ(ha, hb), "of", len(ha) * 8)
blocks.out:
2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824
04a6f55face2f46be8c23f627d539827615851e10751b63ec59db6d2c706b770
input bits that differ:  1
output bits that differ: 127 of 256

blocks.text: The everyday use is checking that a download is exactly what the publisher released. macOS ships `shasum` (and `openssl dgst`).     Compare the digest you compute with the one on the project's website or in its signed release notes:

blocks.code:
$ printf 'hello' | shasum -a 256
2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824  -
$ printf 'hello' > a.txt && shasum -a 256 a.txt > SHA256SUMS
$ cat SHA256SUMS
2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824  a.txt
$ shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS
a.txt: OK
$ printf 'hellO' > a.txt && shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS
a.txt: FAILED
shasum: WARNING: 1 computed checksum did NOT match

blocks.title: Which hash
A hash proves integrity, not origin

blocks.text: If an attacker can replace the download, they can replace the checksum on the same page too. A hash only helps when you get     it through a channel you trust more than the file: a signed release, a different site, or a package manager that checks signatures for     you (Homebrew and pip verify hashes of what they download).
Passwords need slow hashes

Storing `sha256(password)` looks safe and is not. SHA-256 is designed to be *fast*: a single graphics card computes billions of     them per second, so an attacker who steals your database tries every common password against every hash in minutes. Two fixes, always     together: a random **salt** per user (so identical passwords give different hashes and precomputed tables are useless) and a     deliberately **slow, memory-hard** function, so each guess costs real time and memory.

head: Function
Tunable cost
Recommendation
rows: the first choice for new systems (winner of the Password Hashing Competition, RFC 9106)
good; built into Python's `hashlib` on macOS and Linux
fine and very widely supported; truncates passwords at 72 bytes
acceptable when you need FIPS compliance; OWASP suggests 600,000 iterations
blocks.title: Password hashing

blocks.text: The browser has PBKDF2 built in. Run this and change the iteration count: the time grows in proportion, which is the whole     point. The fixed salt is only so the output is the same every time; real code generates a random one per password and stores it next     to the hash.
Change `1000` to `600000` in all three calls and run again: the pause you notice is the work every single guess now costs an     attacker.

On your Mac, Python's `hashlib.scrypt` and `hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac` are available because the system Python and Homebrew Python are     built with OpenSSL. (The in-page Python is not, which is why the box above uses the browser.) For a real application use a library such     as `argon2-cffi`, which picks safe parameters and stores them inside the hash string:

blocks.code:
import hashlib, hmac, os

def hash_password(password: str) -> str:
    salt = os.urandom(16)
    digest = hashlib.scrypt(password.encode(), salt=salt, n=2**14, r=8, p=1)
    return f"scrypt$16384$8$1${salt.hex()}${digest.hex()}"

def check_password(password: str, stored: str) -> bool:
    _, n, r, p, salt, digest = stored.split("$")
    candidate = hashlib.scrypt(password.encode(), salt=bytes.fromhex(salt), n=int(n), r=int(r), p=int(p))
    return hmac.compare_digest(candidate.hex(), digest)

stored = hash_password("correct horse battery staple")
print(stored[:40] + "…")
print(check_password("correct horse battery staple", stored), check_password("Tr0ub4dor&3", stored))

blocks.text: MACs: integrity with a shared key

A hash alone cannot prove *who* produced it, because anyone can compute one. Mix a secret key in and you get a **MAC**: only     someone with the key can produce or check the tag. HMAC (RFC 2104) builds a MAC safely from any hash. You already used it to verify     webhooks in the APIs chapter; it also signs AWS API requests, session cookies and JWTs that use `HS256`:

blocks.code:
import base64, hashlib, hmac, json

def b64url(b: bytes) -> str:
    return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()

KEY = b"server-side secret, never sent"
header = b64url(json.dumps({"alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT"}, separators=(",", ":")).encode())
payload = b64url(json.dumps({"sub": "learner", "role": "viewer"}, separators=(",", ":")).encode())
sig = b64url(hmac.new(KEY, f"{header}.{payload}".encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest())
token = f"{header}.{payload}.{sig}"
print(token)

def verify(tok: str) -> bool:
    h, p, s = tok.split(".")
    good = b64url(hmac.new(KEY, f"{h}.{p}".encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest())
    return hmac.compare_digest(good, s)

forged_payload = b64url(json.dumps({"sub": "learner", "role": "admin"}, separators=(",", ":")).encode())
print("original valid:", verify(token))
print("role=admin forgery valid:", verify(f"{header}.{forged_payload}.{sig}"))
blocks.out:
eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJsZWFybmVyIiwicm9sZSI6InZpZXdlciJ9.efvVm9x4Q4BZO5fL7QENRdp2D7bn2K4S8pxUORlXqBg
original valid: True
role=admin forgery valid: False

blocks.text: That is a complete, correct HS256 JWT built by hand. The attacker can read and edit the payload, but without the key cannot make     a matching signature, so promoting `viewer` to `admin` fails. Real servers must also check `exp`, and must refuse a token whose header     says `"alg": "none"`: a famous class of bugs came from libraries that believed the header.
Symmetric encryption: AES-GCM

**Symmetric** encryption uses one key to encrypt and decrypt. AES is the block cipher almost everything uses, with hardware     support in every Apple chip. On its own a block cipher encrypts 16 bytes; a **mode** turns it into something useful, and today the     right mode is an **AEAD** (authenticated encryption with associated data) such as **AES-GCM** or **ChaCha20-Poly1305**. An AEAD takes a     key, a **nonce** (number used once) and a message, and returns ciphertext plus a 16-byte **tag**. Decryption checks the tag first and     refuses to return anything if a single bit changed.

blocks.code:
key (32 bytes, secret) ──┐
nonce (12 bytes, unique) ┼──▶ ⟪b:AES-GCM encrypt⟫ ──▶ ciphertext (same length) + ⟪g:tag⟫ (16 bytes)
plaintext ───────────────┘
                                ⟪b:AES-GCM decrypt⟫ ──▶ plaintext   ⟪d:if the tag verifies⟫
                                                 └──▶ ⟪r:error⟫       ⟪d:otherwise: no partial output⟫
store or send: nonce ‖ ciphertext ‖ tag   (the nonce is not secret; it must never repeat for the same key)

blocks.text: Use the AES-GCM tab of the cipher lab above to encrypt with a password, tamper with one bit and watch decryption refuse. The same steps in code, with a fixed key so the output is repeatable:

blocks.out:
plaintext  19 bytes
ciphertext 610bd57c0d6eb49fb3ed33e1f471c4a99b6cbd
tag        e7ef675752f0784676176284d0f9f85f
decrypted: nas backup at 02:00
tampered:  OperationError

blocks.text: Why "never reuse a nonce"? GCM encrypts by XORing the message with a keystream that depends only on the key and the nonce.     Encrypt two messages with the same pair and the keystream cancels out: XORing the two ciphertexts gives the XOR of the two     plaintexts, and if the attacker knows or guesses one message, they read the other. Reuse also lets them forge tags. Watch it happen:

The attacker recovers as many bytes as they guessed (here all but the final `!`, because the guessed request is one byte     shorter). The fix is boring and absolute: generate a fresh random 12-byte nonce with `crypto.getRandomValues` (or `os.urandom(12)`) for every     message, or use a library that does it for you. With random nonces, rotate the key long before 2³² messages.

For a file you want to keep private, use a tool whose defaults are already right. `age` (`brew install age`) encrypts with a     password (`age -p -o notes.txt.age notes.txt`) or to someone's public key, using modern authenticated encryption. Avoid     `openssl enc`: its CBC modes have no authentication tag, so a changed file decrypts to garbage instead of being rejected, and its options     make weak choices easy. For whole disks, FileVault already does this with AES-XTS on every Mac.
Public-key cryptography: key exchange and signatures

Symmetric encryption has one big problem: both sides need the same secret key, and you cannot send it over the network you are     trying to protect. Public-key (asymmetric) cryptography solves it with key **pairs**: a private key you never share and a public key you     give to everyone. Two operations matter in practice.
Key exchange

Diffie-Hellman lets two parties who have never met agree on a shared secret while an eavesdropper watches every message. Each side     keeps a secret number, sends a value derived from it, and combines the other side's value with its own secret. Both reach the same     result; the eavesdropper would have to solve the discrete logarithm problem. Try it with small numbers, then let Eve attack:

blocks.code:
import secrets

p = 2**127 - 1                       # a Mersenne prime, big enough for a demo, far too small for real use
g = 3
a = secrets.randbelow(p - 3) + 2     # Alice's secret
b = secrets.randbelow(p - 3) + 2     # Bob's secret
A, B = pow(g, a, p), pow(g, b, p)    # sent in public
alice_key, bob_key = pow(B, a, p), pow(A, b, p)
print("A and B fit in 127 bits:", A.bit_length() <= 127 and B.bit_length() <= 127)
print("same secret on both sides:", alice_key == bob_key)
blocks.out:
A and B fit in 127 bits: True
same secret on both sides: True

blocks.text: Real systems use **elliptic-curve** Diffie-Hellman, usually **X25519**, where 32-byte keys give the security of much larger classic     numbers, and both sides feed the shared secret into a key-derivation function to get the actual AES keys. Because a quantum computer     could one day solve both discrete-log problems, the internet is moving to **hybrid** key exchange: X25519 combined with ML-KEM, a     post-quantum algorithm standardised by NIST in 2024. Chrome, Edge and Firefox already offer `X25519MLKEM768` in TLS, and Apple's TLS     stack, which Safari uses, has offered it since macOS 26 and iOS 26.
Signatures

A **signature** is made with a private key and checked with the public key. It proves that the holder of the private key approved     exactly these bytes. It is how your Mac knows an app came from its developer, how Git hosts mark commits as verified, how package     managers trust updates, and how a TLS server proves its identity. Ed25519 is the modern default:

blocks.out:
public key: 32 bytes
signature:  64 bytes
genuine:   true
tampered:  false

blocks.text: Your SSH key is an Ed25519 key pair too, and OpenSSH can sign and verify files with it (`ssh-keygen -Y`), the same mechanism     Git uses to sign commits with `git config gpg.format ssh`. This transcript is a real run; your fingerprint will differ:

blocks.code:
$ ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "learner@mac" -f ~/.ssh/id_lab
Generating public/private ed25519 key pair.
Enter passphrase (empty for no passphrase):
Enter same passphrase again:
Your identification has been saved in /Users/learner/.ssh/id_lab
Your public key has been saved in /Users/learner/.ssh/id_lab.pub
The key fingerprint is:
SHA256:D3GZuVzJm2EQTXV4Jl0NxcA6rISiWMZInk9GkZZ5EEA learner@mac
$ ssh-keygen -Y sign -f ~/.ssh/id_lab -n file notes.txt
Signing file notes.txt
Write signature to notes.txt.sig
$ echo "learner@mac $(cat ~/.ssh/id_lab.pub)" > allowed_signers
$ ssh-keygen -Y verify -f allowed_signers -I learner@mac -n file -s notes.txt.sig < notes.txt
Good "file" signature for learner@mac with ED25519 key SHA256:D3GZuVzJm2EQTXV4Jl0NxcA6rISiWMZInk9GkZZ5EEA
$ echo 'one more line' >> notes.txt
$ ssh-keygen -Y verify -f allowed_signers -I learner@mac -n file -s notes.txt.sig < notes.txt
Signature verification failed: incorrect signature
Could not verify signature.

blocks.text: The `-n file` **namespace** is part of what gets signed, so a signature made for one purpose (say `git`) cannot be replayed as a     signature for another. Protect a private key with a passphrase, and on a Mac let the Keychain remember it (`ssh-add --apple-use-keychain`).
Certificates and TLS

A public key alone does not say *whose* key it is. A **certificate** binds a public key to a name (`app.lab.example`), with an     expiry date, signed by a **certificate authority** (CA). Your Mac and browsers ship with a list of trusted root CAs. A server sends its     certificate plus any **intermediate** certificates, and the client checks the chain up to a root it already trusts, then checks the     name and the dates.

blocks.code:
⟪w:root CA⟫  (in your Mac's trust store, offline, valid for decades)
   │ signs
⟪w:intermediate CA⟫  (does the daily signing)
   │ signs
⟪b:app.lab.example⟫  public key + names + notBefore/notAfter   ◀── sent by the server in the TLS handshake
   └── the server proves it holds the matching private key by signing the handshake (CertificateVerify)

blocks.text: Certificates are getting shorter-lived so that a stolen key or a mistake expires quickly. Under rules adopted by the CA/Browser     Forum, publicly trusted certificates could be valid for at most 200 days from 15 March 2026; the limit drops to 100 days on 15 March 2027     and 47 days on 15 March 2029. Let's Encrypt certificates already last 90 days. The practical consequence: renewal must be automatic     (certbot, Caddy, your cloud's certificate manager), because nobody remembers to do it by hand eight times a year.
Now watch a full TLS 1.3 handshake, including what an eavesdropper still sees:
Lab: your own certificate authority

The best way to understand chains is to build one. You will create a private root CA, issue a certificate for `localhost` and     `127.0.0.1`, serve HTTPS with Python, and watch curl reject it until you tell curl to trust your CA. Everything stays in `~/lab/ca`.     macOS's own `openssl` is LibreSSL; use Homebrew's OpenSSL 3 for this lab so the commands and output match:

blocks.code:
brew install openssl@3
alias ossl="$(brew --prefix openssl@3)/bin/openssl"
mkdir -p ~/lab/ca && cd ~/lab/ca
ossl version

blocks.text: Create the root CA: a P-256 key and a self-signed certificate valid for ten years.

blocks.code:
ossl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out ca.key
ossl req -x509 -new -key ca.key -sha256 -days 3650 -subj "/CN=Lab Root CA" -out ca.crt

blocks.text: Create the server key and a certificate signing request, then sign it with the CA. The extension file lists the names the certificate is valid for: browsers ignore the CN and check only the subjectAltName.

blocks.code:
ossl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out server.key
printf 'subjectAltName=DNS:lab.localhost,DNS:localhost,IP:127.0.0.1\nextendedKeyUsage=serverAuth\nbasicConstraints=CA:FALSE\n' > server.ext
ossl req -new -key server.key -subj "/CN=lab.localhost" -out server.csr
ossl x509 -req -in server.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -days 30 -sha256 -extfile server.ext -out server.crt

blocks.text: Inspect and verify what you made. This output is from OpenSSL 3.0; newer versions print names without the spaces around `=`:

blocks.code:
$ ossl x509 -in server.crt -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
subject=CN = lab.localhost
issuer=CN = Lab Root CA
notBefore=Nov 16 23:27:53 2026 GMT
notAfter=Dec 16 23:27:53 2026 GMT
X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:
    DNS:lab.localhost, DNS:localhost, IP Address:127.0.0.1
$ ossl verify -CAfile ca.crt server.crt
server.crt: OK
$ ossl verify server.crt
CN = lab.localhost
error 20 at 0 depth lookup: unable to get local issuer certificate
error server.crt: verification failed

blocks.text: Serve HTTPS with the new certificate. Save this next to the keys and run it in its own tab:

blocks.code:
import http.server, ssl

ctx = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER)
ctx.load_cert_chain("server.crt", "server.key")
srv = http.server.HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8443), http.server.SimpleHTTPRequestHandler)
srv.socket = ctx.wrap_socket(srv.socket, server_side=True)
print("Serving https://localhost:8443/", flush=True)
srv.serve_forever()

blocks.text: Then connect from a second tab. curl refuses until you give it the CA, exactly as a browser would refuse an unknown issuer:

blocks.code:
$ echo 'hello over TLS' > index.html
$ curl -sS https://localhost:8443/
curl: (60) SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate
More details here: https://curl.se/docs/sslcerts.html

curl failed to verify the legitimacy of the server and therefore could not
establish a secure connection to it. To learn more about this situation and
how to fix it, please visit the web page mentioned above.
$ curl -sS --cacert ca.crt https://localhost:8443/
hello over TLS
$ echo | ossl s_client -connect localhost:8443 -servername localhost -CAfile ca.crt -brief
CONNECTION ESTABLISHED
Protocol version: TLSv1.3
Ciphersuite: TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
Peer certificate: CN = lab.localhost
Hash used: SHA256
Signature type: ECDSA
Verification: OK
Server Temp Key: X25519, 253 bits
DONE

items.text: **`Server Temp Key: X25519`** is the ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key for this connection only: steal the server key next year and you still cannot decrypt today's recording. That property is **forward secrecy**, and TLS 1.3 always has it.
**`Signature type: ECDSA`** is the server proving it holds the private key of the certificate, the CertificateVerify step in the widget.
**Exit code 60** is curl's "certificate problem" code. Scripts should treat it as fatal, never retry with `-k`.

blocks.title: Keep the CA key off everything that matters

blocks.text: Anyone with `ca.key` can mint a certificate for any name. If you add `ca.crt` to your Mac's System keychain as trusted (Keychain     Access, or `sudo security add-trusted-cert`), a stolen `ca.key` could impersonate your bank to your own browser. For local development,     `mkcert` (`brew install mkcert`) automates this lab with name constraints and sensible defaults; delete lab CAs from the keychain when you     are done.

blocks.name: openssl req
blocks.sum: Create keys, certificate signing requests and self-signed or CA-signed certificates.
blocks.syntax:
openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out KEY
openssl req -new|-x509 -key KEY -subj "/CN=NAME" -out FILE
openssl x509 -req -in CSR -CA CA.crt -CAkey CA.key -extfile EXT -out CRT

how.text: `genpkey` makes a private key. `req -new` wraps the public half and your requested names into a **certificate signing request** (CSR), signed with the private key to prove you hold it. `req -x509` skips the CA and signs the certificate with the same key: a **self-signed** certificate, which is what a root CA is.

`x509 -req` is the CA side: it reads a CSR and signs a certificate with the CA key. The extensions file decides what the certificate is good for: `subjectAltName` lists the DNS names and IPs (clients check only this, not the CN), `basicConstraints=CA:FALSE` stops the certificate from signing others, and `extendedKeyUsage=serverAuth` limits it to TLS servers.
Public CAs such as Let's Encrypt run this same process automatically through the ACME protocol, after proving you control the domain.

flags.d: a P-256 key; `-algorithm ed25519` also works for many uses

make a self-signed certificate valid for N days
sign a CSR as a CA

examples.desc: A throwaway self-signed certificate for localhost
examples.code: openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -nodes -keyout key.pem -out cert.pem -days 7 -subj "/CN=localhost" -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:localhost,IP:127.0.0.1"

examples.desc: Show the names a certificate is valid for

gotchas: A certificate without subjectAltName is rejected by browsers and modern curl even when the CN matches.
Private keys written by these commands are unencrypted unless you ask otherwise. Keep them out of Git and readable only by you (`chmod 600`).

blocks.name: ssh-keygen -Y
blocks.sum: Sign files with an SSH key and verify those signatures, with no extra tools.
blocks.syntax:
ssh-keygen -Y sign -f KEY -n NAMESPACE FILE
ssh-keygen -Y verify -f ALLOWED_SIGNERS -I IDENTITY -n NAMESPACE -s FILE.sig < FILE

how.text: OpenSSH (built into macOS) can make detached signatures with the same Ed25519 key you use to log in. `sign` writes `FILE.sig`; `verify` reads the data on standard input and checks the signature against an **allowed signers** file that maps identities to public keys.

The **namespace** (`-n file`, `-n git`, or your own) is signed too, so a signature made for one purpose cannot be reused for another. Git uses exactly this mechanism when you set `gpg.format ssh` and sign commits.

flags.d: sign FILE with private key KEY in namespace NS
verify standard input against SIG for identity ID
find which identity in SIGNERS made a signature
generate a new Ed25519 key pair

examples.desc: Verify it and print only the result line
examples.code: ssh-keygen -Y verify -f allowed_signers -I {{user}}@mac -n file -s notes.txt.sig < notes.txt 2>&1 | head -1

gotchas: `verify` reads the signed data from standard input, not from a file argument: forgetting the `< FILE` makes it wait for typing.

blocks.text: Secrets in daily work

items.text: **Passwords**: a password manager and a unique generated password per site. Apple's Passwords app is enough. Reuse is the attack that actually happens.
**API keys and tokens**: in the Keychain (`security add-generic-password`), a secret manager, or environment variables loaded from a file that `.gitignore` excludes. Never in code, never in a URL.
**SSH and signing keys**: Ed25519, with a passphrase, one key per device so you can revoke one without the others.
**Random values**: `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` in Python or `crypto.getRandomValues` in JavaScript. Never `random` or `Math.random()` for anything security-related; they are predictable.
**When something leaks**: revoke and rotate first, investigate second. Deleting a commit does not un-leak a key that was pushed.

blocks.title: Pick the right tool

task.text: For each job, name the tool (encoding, hash, slow password hash, MAC, authenticated encryption, signature, or TLS) and one concrete        algorithm: (a) store user passwords for a web app; (b) prove a downloaded installer is unmodified, given a checksum on a signed release        page; (c) let a provider prove a webhook came from them, using a secret you both know; (d) publish a file that anyone can verify came        from you, without sharing any secret; (e) keep a backup file private on a cloud drive; (f) put binary data inside a JSON string.

hints: Ask two questions: does anyone need to read it back, and does the verifier share a secret with the producer?
blocks.solution:
(a) slow password hash: Argon2id (or scrypt, bcrypt) with a per-user salt
(b) hash: SHA-256, compared with the published checksum
(c) MAC: HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body
(d) signature: Ed25519 (for example ssh-keygen -Y sign, or minisign)
(e) authenticated encryption: AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, for example with age
(f) encoding: base64 (no security at all, and that is fine for this job)

why.text: Each tool answers one question. Passwords need to be checked, never read back, and must resist guessing: slow hash. Integrity        with a shared secret is a MAC; integrity without one is a signature. Privacy needs encryption, and only authenticated encryption also        detects tampering. Base64 is for transport, not protection.

blocks.title: SHA-256 in the browser

task.text: Write `async function sha256hex(text)` that returns the SHA-256 digest of the UTF-8 bytes of `text` as a lowercase hex string,        using `crypto.subtle.digest`. Inside an `async` function `main`, print the digest of `hello` and call `main()`.

hints: `digest` returns an `ArrayBuffer`; wrap it in `Uint8Array` and format each byte with `toString(16).padStart(2, '0')`.

why.text: Web Crypto works on bytes, not strings, and returns raw bytes, so every real use has the same two conversions at the edges.        `padStart` matters: without it, a byte such as `0x0a` becomes `a` and the hex string is too short and wrong.

questions.q: A system stores `base64(password)`. How protected are the passwords?

options.text: Not at all: anyone can decode base64
Protected unless the attacker has a quantum computer

questions.why: Encoding has no key. It is a representation, not a protection.

questions.q: Why is SHA-256 a poor choice for storing passwords on its own?

options.text: It is fast, so stolen hashes can be guessed at billions per second

questions.why: SHA-256 is a fine hash, but password storage needs a salt and a deliberately slow function such as Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt.

questions.q: What does AES-GCM decryption do if one bit of the ciphertext changed?

options.text: Returns plaintext with one wrong character
Returns plaintext with one wrong block
Refuses: the tag check fails and no plaintext is returned

questions.why: GCM is authenticated encryption. The tag covers every bit, and decryption is all or nothing.

questions.q: Two messages were encrypted with AES-GCM using the same key and the same nonce. What can an attacker do?

options.text: Nothing; the key is still secret
XOR the ciphertexts to get the XOR of the plaintexts, and forge tags
Decrypt any past message with the key

questions.why: The keystream depends only on key and nonce, so it cancels out. Never reuse a nonce with the same key.

questions.q: In TLS 1.3, what lets a client know the server really holds the private key for its certificate?

options.text: The CertificateVerify signature over the handshake transcript

questions.why: Anyone can send a copy of a public certificate. Only the key holder can sign this handshake's transcript.

questions.q: Your `curl` fails with exit code 60 against your own lab server. The right fix?

options.text: Give curl the CA that signed the server certificate with `--cacert`

questions.why: `-k` turns off the check that makes HTTPS meaningful. Trust the specific CA instead.

blocks.title: vault: an encrypted, signed notes file

blocks.text: Write `vault.py`, a small command-line tool that keeps a notes file encrypted at rest with a password, detects tampering, and can             publish a signed copy. It uses the `cryptography` package (`python3 -m pip install cryptography` in your project's virtual             environment), which wraps OpenSSL with safe, high-level APIs.
1. The file format

Write one line of JSON: `{"v": 1, "kdf": "scrypt", "n": 32768, "r": 8, "p": 1, "salt": "…", "nonce": "…", "ct": "…"}` with base64             values. Putting the parameters in the file means you can raise them later without breaking old vaults.
2. Encrypt and decrypt

Derive a 32-byte key with `hashlib.scrypt` (with `n=32768` also pass `maxmem=64 * 1024 * 1024`, because the default memory limit is too small), then seal the notes with `cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead.AESGCM` and a fresh             `os.urandom(12)` nonce on every save. Pass the JSON header (without `ct`) as **associated data**, so changing the parameters is detected             too. `vault.py edit` decrypts to a temporary file, opens `$EDITOR`, and re-encrypts on exit.
3. Prove tampering is caught
Flip one character in the `ct` field with a text editor and confirm `vault.py show` reports an authentication failure (`InvalidTag`) and prints nothing else.
4. Publish a signed export

`vault.py export notes.txt` writes the plaintext and signs it with your SSH key via `ssh-keygen -Y sign -n file` (call it with             `subprocess`). `vault.py verify notes.txt` runs `ssh-keygen -Y verify` against an `allowed_signers` file. Commit the public key so             others can verify your exports.
5. Stretch goals

items.text: Support changing the password without re-encrypting the notes: encrypt a random data key with the password-derived key (this is **envelope encryption**, exactly how cloud key services work).
Store the password in the Keychain with `security` so `vault.py` can run unattended, and discuss what that changes about your threat model.

terms.def: a one-way function giving a fixed-size digest; any change to the input changes the digest
random bytes stored with a password hash so equal passwords hash differently
message authentication code: a tag computed with a shared secret key that proves integrity and origin
a standard way to build a MAC from a hash function such as SHA-256
authenticated encryption with associated data, such as AES-GCM: encrypts and detects tampering
a number used once; must never repeat with the same key in AES-GCM
a protocol, such as (EC)DH, by which two parties derive a shared secret over a public channel
stealing a long-term key later does not expose sessions recorded earlier, because each session used an ephemeral key
a value made with a private key that anyone can verify with the matching public key
a signed statement binding a public key to names, valid for a period, issued by a certificate authority
certificate authority: an entity whose signature on a certificate clients trust
Server Name Indication: the host name a TLS client asks for, sent in clear in the ClientHello
